newsitem.title: USA: Dlr climbs after US open on trade, orbits 114 yen.
newsitem.headline: Dlr climbs after US open on trade, orbits 114 yen.

text.p: The dollar opened higher then climbed even further after news of a surprisingly large drop in the U.S. international trade deficit, experts said.
The overall trade shortfall shrank 19.3 percent to $8.51 billion in March. Economists polled by Reuters, on average, had expected the March trade gap to fall to $10.3 billion.
The politically sensitive trade deficit with Japan rose 8.3 percent to $4.61 billion in March.
"Well, it's the best of all worlds," said Mike Malpede, a senior foreign exchange analyst at REFCO Group Ltd.
He was referring to the trade report.
Malpede ticked off a number of positives gleaned from the trade data: "We have record exports. We had trade improvement. There's only a slight problem with Japan..."
Malpede concluded that the trade report showed the U.S. economy is strong and the decline in the dollar on Tuesday was a "joke".
U.S.exports shot up 4.1 percent in March, boosted by sales of aircraft and nonmonetary gold.
The dollar had sold off sharply on Tuesday after the Federal Reserve announced it left interest rates unchanged.
The dollar opened at 1.6870/80 marks and 113.60/70 yen, up from 1.6765/75 marks and 112.58/68 yen at Tuesday's close.
Shortly after the trade data hit the market, the greenback surged above 1.69 marks and repeatedly poked above 114 yen.
Chris Turner, a research director at I.D.E.A. Inc, pegged good dollar resistance at 114.80 yen, which he described as a "big breakdown" area on a previous move lower.
Prior to release of the trade data, the dollar had strengthened following a flurry of comments from overseas, according to analysts.

The Swiss National Bank (SNB) said the recent upward pressure on the Swiss franc was without any fundamental reason. Moreover, the SNB said it had reacted by significantly adding liquidity to the money markets.

The dollar opened at 1.4060/70 Swiss francs, up from 1.3860/70 francs at the prior close. The mark also gained against the Swiss unit, trading near 0.8334/36 francs shortly after the open compared with 0.8319/22 in early dealings.
The strong statement and physical move from the SNB really took pressure off the downside of the dollar and enabled dollar/Swiss to lead the dollar back up, Turner said.
In Asia, Takahiro Kawase, director of the Bank Of Japan's (BOJ) policy planning department, told reporters that the central bank has no plans for an immediate rate rise.
Separately, Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a parliamentary committee that Japanese politicians should refrain from commenting on interest rates.
Mitsuzuka also said worries over an excessive weakening of the yen have completely disappeared.
Members of Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party recently made remarks calling for a rise in the official discount rate, which has remained at a record low 0.5 percent.
"It seems like (Japanese officials are) trying to do a job of taking the rate hike scenario out of the picture and maybe taking some of the pressure off the yen's upside at the moment," Turner said.

A key Bundesbank official also joined the chorus of those making comments from overseas. Buba council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick said he had little objection to dollar/mark around 1.70 but saw no need to expect further weakness of the mark against the dollar.

"I think that's just some type of minor damage control by the Bundesbank in terms of saying...it may have gone too far when it shot below in the overnight with the dollar/yen," said Hillel Waxman, a first vice president at Bank Leumi Trust Co of New York.
In other trade, the dollar opened at Canadian $1.3662/67, down from C$1.3667/72. Sterling slid to $1.6525/35 from $1.6560/70. The Australian dollar opened at $0.7775/80, up from $0.7739/44.
((-- Donna Sells, N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1668))
